(a) Cell membrane: lipids and proteins
(b) Fungal cell wall: chitin
(c) Plant cell wall: cellulose
(d) Bacterial cell wall: peptidoglycan (murein)
(e) Ribosomes: RNA and proteins
(f) Chromosomes: DNA and proteins

The fluid mosaic model describes a flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it. Lipids and many proteins can move sideways, giving the membrane fluidity, while the varied proteins form a mosaic. The membrane is selectively permeable and regulates movement of substances into and out of the cell.

The cell wall is a rigid, non-living layer outside the cell membrane. Plant cell walls are mainly cellulose, fungal walls contain chitin, and bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan. The wall supports and protects the cell, helps maintain its shape and prevents it from bursting when water enters.

The nucleus has a double membrane with pores and contains nucleoplasm, chromatin and a nucleolus. The pores regulate transport; chromatin contains DNA and proteins and condenses into chromosomes; the nucleolus assembles ribosome components.

Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing digestive enzymes that break down waste, foreign materials and worn-out cell parts. The endoplasmic reticulum is a membrane network: rough ER bears ribosomes and helps synthesize and transport proteins, while smooth ER lacks ribosomes and synthesizes lipids and helps detoxify harmful substances.

The Golgi complex consists of stacks of flattened membrane-bound sacs called cisternae. It receives proteins and other materials from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies and sorts them, and packages them into vesicles for transport or secretion.

A chloroplast has a double membrane and chlorophyll in its thylakoid membranes. Thylakoids form stacks called grana within the stroma. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, using light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water and releasing oxygen.
Water enters a plant cell by osmosis and the vacuole swells. The cell contents press against the cell wall, which resists the pressure; this creates turgor pressure and makes the cell firm.

Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and usually one large central vacuole; animal cells lack a cell wall and chloroplasts and generally have smaller vacuoles or none. Plant cells usually have a more regular shape, while animal cells are generally more flexible and irregular.

Division of labour is the specialization of different cells, tissues and organs to perform different functions, making an organism work efficiently. Examples include red blood cells transporting oxygen, nerve cells carrying signals, muscle cells contracting for movement, xylem transporting water and mesophyll cells carrying out photosynthesis.

Cell specialization is the development of structures suited to particular functions. It enables division of labour in multicellular organisms; for example, nerve cells transmit signals, red blood cells transport oxygen and mesophyll cells carry out photosynthesis.
Mitochondrial dysfunction or absence would reduce the cell's ATP supply. Energy-dependent processes in other organelles and at the cell membrane could slow or stop, impairing normal cell activities.

If coordination failed, ribosomes might not receive or use the nucleus's genetic instructions correctly, disrupting protein synthesis. Missing or faulty proteins, including enzymes and structural proteins, would impair cell activities. The nucleus stores the instructions, and ribosomes use them to make proteins.
